messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Liam Weber was 26 when a flash flood tore through the campground where he, his wife, and her young niece had gone for a weekend trip. The rain had been hard all afternoon, but he had told himself they would be fine. By nightfall the water came fast, carrying mud, branches, and pieces of shattered gear through the cabins. What stayed with him were not clean, orderly memories but broken flashes: the sour smell of soaked clothes and sweat in the crush of bodies trying to move uphill, a child screaming for her mother, his wife slipping from his grasp in the dark water. When he tries to describe that night now, he stops and stares at the floor. He knows what happened, but the words will not come in sequence. Instead, the scene returns like a film clip that starts before he is ready and repeats without finishing.

In the months after the flood, those fragments began attaching themselves to ordinary moments. At work as a salesperson in a busy home improvement store, the smell of a customer’s body odour after a long day in the heat can pull him straight back into the panic of the evacuation. If children come through his aisle, especially if one calls out loudly or starts to cry, the memory jumps forward in disconnected pieces—the small hand he could not keep hold of, the noise, the water. Even talking about the flood in the break room is enough to set the replay going. Each time this happens, Liam’s mind lands on the same conclusion: he was inadequate when it mattered most. He had come to believe that if he had been stronger, faster, more capable, his wife might still be alive.

That belief has hardened rather than softened. The more the memories replay in fragments, the more certain he becomes that something in him failed catastrophically. He also cannot stop circling around the fact that no one, in his view, has really been held accountable: the campground reopened, the warnings had been poor, and life seemed to continue for everyone else. The event feels unfinished, senseless. From there it does not take much for him to think, with bitter conviction, that he cannot deal with even minor upset now. A delayed text, a late delivery, a coworker not showing up on time—small disruptions feel like proof that he is already near the edge.

That sense of fragility has shaped how he lives. Liam tries hard to control his emotions, especially around other people. If he feels himself getting tight in the chest or watery-eyed, he clamps down, changes the subject, or leaves the room. He avoids grief reminders with a carefulness that has grown over time: he keeps his wife’s photo turned face down on a shelf, takes a longer route through town to avoid the park where they used to walk, and will not look at camping displays in the store unless he has to. At home he sometimes drifts off into elaborate fantasy, losing himself in imagined versions of life where the trip was canceled or the water never rose. Those habits give him brief distance, but they also leave the loss and the flood strangely unprocessed, so that the memory returns in the same jagged, wordless form. Afterward he feels even more defective for not being able to face what happened directly.

The replaying memories have also changed his sense of safety. Because they arrive so suddenly and vividly, he stays on guard even inside his apartment, checking the windows during storms and listening for changes in the weather app notification tone on his phone. He is quick to anger in ways that embarrass him: snapping at a neighbor over hallway noise, slamming a cabinet when an online order runs late, barking at a customer who asked for help while a child tugged at the cart nearby. Delays are especially hard. If his manager is late back from lunch or a friend does not answer right away, Liam is certain something bad is happening. In that keyed-up state, he scans more intensely for signs of danger, and the very things he is watching for—children’s voices, sweat, any conversation about the flood—stand out immediately and hit harder.

Over time, this constant readiness has fed his view of himself. His irritability and vigilance seem to him like more evidence that he is no longer someone who can cope, just someone damaged and unpredictable. He has started turning down shifts on family-shopping weekends to avoid being around children, and his sales numbers have slipped because he leaves the floor when a smell or conversation catches him off guard. Friends have stopped asking him to join gatherings because he goes silent or disappears. He finally came for help after a storm warning sent him pacing his apartment all night, unable to settle even after the rain passed, and he nearly shouted at a customer’s son the next morning when the boy started crying in his aisle. What frightens Liam most is the thought that this is permanent—that he failed once, broke in the flood, and will stay trapped in that night. What he hopes, though he says it cautiously, is that he might find a way to remember his wife without being pulled under again.
